nameStory: The Banded Graphisurus gets its name from the distinctive bands or stripes that mark its body, making it look like it's wearing a striped shirt. The genus name 'Graphisurus' comes from Greek words meaning 'written tail,' referring to the markings that often extend onto the beetle's rear end like nature's own calligraphy.
description: The Banded Graphisurus is a medium-sized longhorn beetle that's part of a huge family known for their impressively long antennae. Like all longhorn beetles, this species has antennae that are often as long as or longer than their body, giving them an almost alien appearance. They're robust, cylindrical beetles with the characteristic banded pattern that makes them stand out from many of their relatives. Adults typically measure around half an inch to three-quarters of an inch in length.

idTips.label: Distinctive Banding
idTips.description: Look for alternating light and dark bands across the wing covers (elytra) that create a striped pattern, often in shades of brown, tan, and darker brown

idTips.label: Long Antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are thread-like and typically extend well beyond the body length, feeling delicate if you gently touch them

idTips.label: Cylindrical Body
idTips.description: Body feels solid and rounded when handled, not flattened like many other beetle families

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Adults are medium-sized for longhorns, roughly the length of your thumbnail from tip to first joint

idTips.label: Robust Build
idTips.description: Has a sturdy, thick-bodied appearance compared to some of the more slender longhorn beetles

habitat: Banded Graphisurus beetles are found in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England, particularly where there are plenty of hardwood trees like oak, maple, and birch. They're often discovered on or near dead and dying trees, fallen logs, and woodpiles since their larvae develop in decaying wood. You might spot adults on flowers, tree bark, or even at porch lights during their active season.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their pupal stage in late spring, but are not yet at peak activity. Look for them starting to appear on tree bark and early spring flowers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity season when adults are most visible, actively mating and laying eggs. This is the best time to spot them on flowers, decaying wood, and flying around outdoor lights at night.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity begins to decline as temperatures drop. Some individuals may still be seen on warm days, but they become increasingly rare.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off and the species overwinters as larvae developing inside dead wood. No adults will be visible during this season.

funFact: Despite being called longhorn 'beetles,' many species in this family, including the Banded Graphisurus, are actually better at using their antennae to 'taste' the air than to hear sounds - those long antennae are packed with chemical receptors that help them find mates and suitable egg-laying sites from surprisingly long distances!
confusionNotes: The banded pattern can sometimes be confused with other striped longhorn beetles, but most other banded longhorns in New England are either much larger or have distinctly different stripe patterns. Remember: if it's medium-sized with clear, regular bands and those characteristic long antennae, you're likely looking at a Banded Graphisurus.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name was established way back in 1775 by the Swedish entomologist Charles De Geer, making this one of the earlier-described North American longhorn beetles. This gives it a long history in scientific literature, though it's not as well-known to the general public as some of its flashier longhorn relatives.
compareHints: Since this is the only Graphisurus species commonly found in New England, compare it to other medium-sized longhorn beetles in the region. Unlike the more common species such as the Red Milkweed Beetle, the Banded Graphisurus lacks bright warning colors and instead relies on its subtle banded camouflage. It's also more robustly built than many of the slender-bodied longhorns you might encounter.
